issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the reported trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations suggests a medical-trauma theme, while avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces suggests transport or confinement-related trauma. Those themes are not supported by the trigger or threat items, which instead center on interpersonal conflict, crying, and hypervigilant safety positioning.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the strategy node, the three avoidance items point to three different situational themes—medical settings, transport, and enclosed spaces—without corresponding support from memory, appraisal, or trigger content. This makes the strategy profile look internally diffuse rather than like a coherent set of coping responses for one trauma formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
issues.explanation: The profile is only partially coherent for childhood physical abuse. Arguments, crying, and conflict avoidance fit the trauma type, but the combination of a highly specific tactile-texture trigger with public transport avoidance and enclosed-space avoidance is difficult to link to this trauma history without any memory or appraisal content explaining that association.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the threat/strategy pattern, back-to-wall positioning and safe-seat seeking imply marked hypervigilance in public or interpersonal environments, which could plausibly connect to transport avoidance, but enclosed-space avoidance suggests a more circumscribed claustrophobic or situational fear that is not otherwise represented in the trigger set.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, and Maladaptive Strategies strongly feed Triggers. Avoiding conflict fits the trigger set (arguments, crying), but avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces target contexts not reflected by the listed triggers, making the node contents insufficiently aligned with the edge pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is not well supported by the rest of the profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. The listed triggers are arguments, crying, and unexpected touch, and the threat items center on interpersonal vigilance and positioning in rooms. Public transport avoidance suggests a different trigger/threat context and is hard to link coherently to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is not clearly connected to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance in shared spaces and interpersonal danger cues, while the triggers are interpersonal/emotional and tactile. Being alone as a primary avoidance target pulls toward a different clinical pattern unless there were accompanying abandonment or panic-related items, which are absent here.

Difficulty concentrating is a nonspecific PTSD symptom rather than a threat appraisal/perceived current danger item. Within this node, the other threat items specifically reflect situational safety behaviors and surveillance of the environment. This item does not fit the node's theme and weakens alignment with the formulation in which Threat is tightly linked to Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette: Tariq was nine when his father's hands became unpredictable. What began as strict discipline quickly shifted into a pattern of sudden grabs and shoves that left bruises on his forearms, alongside shouts that vibrated through the thin walls of their house. He learned to track the subtle shifts in his father's posture, the tightness around the eyes, the way a raised voice always preceded physical contact. When his mother would break down in tears, the sound didn't offer solace; it simply marked another moment of chaos. Those childhood years left him with a constant, low-grade awareness that danger could arrive without warning, and that silence was the only reliable buffer. Over time, a set of routines settled into his daily life. He stopped engaging in disagreements of any kind, even when his wife, Leila, offered a different perspective on their shared schedules or their budget. He would go quiet, shift his posture, and steer the conversation toward safer topics, because he had come to believe that any exchange of opposing views would inevitably spiral out of control. He also found himself needing company in almost every setting. Being alone in a room or a building made his breathing grow shallow, so he would sit in hallways near the laboratory breakroom, or he would text Leila to join him on the couch while he reviewed reports. He began stepping back from departmental mixers and skipping Friday afternoon drinks with lab mates, telling people he had family commitments instead. He avoided other people not out of indifference, but because their presence felt inherently unpredictable. In his current work as an environmental scientist at a regional water quality firm, these patterns co-existed with his professional responsibilities. His role required weekly data reviews in a glass-walled conference room and biweekly field sampling trips across the county. In the office, he always claimed the corner table, positioning his chair so his back rested firmly against the wall and his gaze covered the entire space. He studied the faces and shoulders of his supervisors and peers as they spoke, tracking every shift in expression or stance for signs of tension. During site visits, he kept a careful distance from his colleagues. When a field technician reached out unprepared to adjust a sensor on his vest, Tariq jerked backward, dropping his notebook into the gravel. Later, when two project managers began debating a sampling protocol in the conference room, the sound of their voices made his shoulders lock. He packed his bag, excused himself, and left for the day, telling Leila he needed to avoid the noise. He hadn't told anyone how stillness and silence had become his only reliable comforts, or how he constantly calculated his position in every room to ensure he could see who entered. The fatigue of living this way had accumulated over recent months. He knew his social and professional schedule was shrinking, but the thought of testing his own boundaries felt more dangerous than the avoidance itself. He remembered how his own voice had trembled during a disagreement with Leila, and how quickly he had shut down, certain that any escalation would mirror the chaos of his childhood. He hadn't spoken about the way loud discussions still made his chest tighten, or how hearing crying anywhere nearby brought back a heavy, unplaceable dread. He came to therapy because the quiet routines were no longer enough to carry him through the workday. He hoped to find a way to sit in a meeting without checking the walls, to hear a raised voice without bracing his body, and to trust that not every unfamiliar touch carried the weight of his past. He wanted to understand why his body still reacted as though danger were present, even when the lab was empty and Leila was sitting quietly beside him.
